deep.reconstruction:
Chapter XV of Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, 'On the divisors of numbers of the form xx+yy', §§542–551. The page sets up the lemma that is completed on the next page: if a prime a²+b² divides p²+q², then the quotient is again a sum of two squares.

§541–542. Assume gcd(x,y)=1, since a common factor φ only contributes φ². If x and y are both odd, then x²+y² ≡ 2 (mod 4). So x²+y² can be prime only in the case 2=1+1.

§543. Take one of x, y even and the other odd. Then x²+y² ≡ 1 (mod 4), so every prime of this form is 4n+1. Since every square is ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4), no number 4n−1 is a sum of two squares.

§544. If x=2p+1 and y=2q+1, then (x²+y²)/2 = 2p²+2p+2q²+2q+1. This equals (p+q+1)²+(p−q)². The two roots sum to 2p+1, which is odd, so one root is even and the other odd. Thus half of such a sum is again a sum of two squares of opposite parity.

§545. Product identity: (a²+b²)(c²+d²) = (ac±bd)²+(ad∓bc)². The two choices of sign give two representations.

§546. Converse problem: if a²+b² divides p²+q², is the quotient a sum of two squares? Euler notes that this does not follow from §545 and needs its own proof.

§547. Reduction step. p²+q² is divisible by D=a²+b² if and only if (p+αD)²+(q+βD)² is, for any integers α, β and either signs. So p and q may be reduced to absolute residues ≤ D/2.

§548. Suppose p=ac+bd and q=ad−bc, so that (p²+q²)/D = c²+d². Shift to p'=p+αD and q'=q+βD. The quotient becomes c²+d²+2α(ac+bd)+2β(ad−bc)+(α²+β²)D. This equals (c+αa−βb)²+(d+αb+βa)². So the property 'quotient is a sum of two squares' survives the reduction of §547.

§549. Euler states the claim for prime D. He remarks that it is true in general, but that the proof should start from the prime case.

§550. Since gcd(a,b)=1, one can write p = ma−nb, and in infinitely many ways. If q = na+mb, then p²+q² = (m²+n²)(a²+b²). Otherwise write q = na+mb+s. Then p²+q² = D(m²+n²) + 2s(na+mb) + s².

§551. Hence D divides s(s+2(na+mb)). Because D is prime, D divides s or D divides s+2(na+mb); this is where primality is used. In the first case put s=tD.

Continuation on the next page, checked:
- Case 1 gives the quotient m²+n²+t(tD+2(na+mb)) = (m+bt)²+(n+at)².
- Case 2: s+2(na+mb) = tD gives (m−bt)²+(n−at)².
This is the first lemma of Euler's descent proof of Fermat's two-squares theorem.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All identities check by expansion.

§543: 'nullus numerus formae 4n−1 ... summa esse potest' is presented as following from the statement about primes ('sicque'). It really follows directly from squares being 0 or 1 mod 4. The conclusion is correct; only the inference wording is loose.

§546/549: the general claim (D composite) is true for integer quotients. For each prime ≡3 mod 4, the exponents in both p²+q² and D are even, so their difference is even. Euler asserts this without proof here, which is acceptable since he only claims it.

results.what: Both x,y odd ⇒ x²+y² ≡ 2 mod 4; primes x²+y² (other than 2) are ≡1 mod 4; no 4n−1 is a sum of two squares.

results.modern_name: Halving identity for sums of two squares

results.what: If a prime a²+b² divides p²+q², the quotient is a sum of two squares; proved via p=ma−nb, q=na+mb+s and Euclid's lemma on s(s+2(na+mb)).
results.modern_name: Euler's first lemma in the descent proof of Fermat's two-squares theorem

results.what: Reduction of p,q modulo D to residues ≤ D/2, and invariance of the 'quotient is sum of two squares' property under shifts.

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known descent proof of the two-squares theorem, as in the Tractatus (published 1849, Opera Posthuma). The parametrization p=ma−nb with a shift s differs slightly from the E228 argument, but it is a minor variant of known Euler material.

checkable.asserts: §548 quotient is a sum of two squares

transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially exactly; the '1'/2' in §547 is ½ as transcribed. No substantive corrections.
